summary.heading: Nuclear fusion
summary.html:
• Fusion: two light nuclei join to form a heavier one. Light nuclei are on the steep side of the binding energy curve, so fusion raises the binding energy per nucleon and releases energy (more per kilogram than fission).
  • The Sun's proton–proton chain, overall: $4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{\;\;0}_{+1}\text{e} + 2\nu_e$, about 26.7 MeV (using atomic masses includes the positrons' annihilation). About 0.7% of the mass becomes energy.
  • Deuterium–tritium fusion (the aim of reactors on Earth) releases 17.6 MeV.
  • Energy released = (mass before − mass after) × 931.5 MeV per u. Also give the change in mass itself (in u, or in kg by multiplying by $1.661 \times 10^{-27}$), and work backwards: the Sun loses mass at $\dfrac{L}{c^2} \approx 4 \times 10^9\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$.

summary.heading: Conditions for fusion and the equilibrium of a star
summary.html:
• Nuclei repel, so to fuse they must get within about $10^{-15}$ m, where the strong force acts. This needs a very high temperature (about $10^7$ K in the Sun's core; matter is a plasma) so they move fast enough, and a very high density so collisions are frequent.
  • In stars, gravity provides both: a collapsing cloud turns gravitational potential energy into thermal energy. On Earth, tokamaks hold plasma above $10^8$ K with magnetic fields.
  • A main-sequence star is stable because gravity (inwards) balances radiation pressure and gas pressure (outwards) at every layer.
  • The balance corrects itself: if the core contracts it heats up, fusion speeds up and pressure pushes it back; if it expands it cools and gravity pulls it back.

summary.heading: Astronomical distances and stellar parallax
summary.html:
UnitMeaningValue
AUmean Earth–Sun distance$1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m
lydistance light travels in a year$9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m
pcdistance at which the parallax angle is 1 arcsecond3.26 ly $= 3.09 \times 10^{16}$ m
$$d\,(\text{parsec}) = \frac{1}{p\,(\text{arcsecond})}$$
  • As the Earth orbits, a nearby star appears to shift against distant stars. The parallax angle $p$ is half the total shift, with a baseline of 1 AU; small-angle approximation $\tan p \approx p$.
  • 1 arcsecond $= \frac{1}{3600}$ of a degree. The smaller $p$, the further the star.
  • Limit: about 100 pc from the ground (atmospheric blurring); space telescopes such as Gaia reach thousands of parsecs.

summary.heading: What starlight tells us and the radius of a star
summary.html:
• Surface temperature from the peak wavelength (Wien's law): $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$ m K.
  • Composition from absorption lines matched with laboratory spectra (E.1): most stars are about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass.
  • Spectral classes O B A F G K M, from hottest (blue, above 30 000 K) to coolest (red, below about 3500 K). The Sun is a G star (about 5800 K).
  • Luminosity from apparent brightness and distance: $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$.
$$L = \sigma AT^4 = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4 \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = \sqrt{\frac{L}{4\pi\sigma T^4}}$$
  • Method: $T$ from Wien's law, $L$ from $b$ and $d$, then $R$. Comparing with the Sun, use ratios: $L \propto R^2T^4$.

summary.heading: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
summary.html:
• Luminosity (vertical, often in units of $L_\odot$) against surface temperature (horizontal), both logarithmic; temperature increases to the left.
RegionProperties
Main sequenceabout 90% of stars, fusing hydrogen to helium; hot, massive and luminous at top left; small red dwarfs at bottom right
Red giantscool but luminous, so large (10–100 $R_\odot$); core hydrogen used up
Supergiantsup to about $10^6 L_\odot$ and 1000 $R_\odot$; from massive stars; red or blue
White dwarfshot but dim, so tiny (about Earth-sized); no fusion, cooling
Instability stripnear-vertical band crossing the main sequence; stars pulsate and their luminosity varies regularly
  • Lines of constant radius slope down from top left to bottom right; up and to the right means bigger stars.
  • A main-sequence star's temperature gives its luminosity from the diagram, and its brightness then gives its distance (beyond parallax range).

summary.heading: How stars evolve
summary.html:
• Nebula collapses under gravity → protostar → hydrogen fusion starts at about $10^7$ K → main sequence (about 90% of its life). What follows depends on mass; massive stars fuse far faster and live much shorter lives.
  • Up to about 8 solar masses: core hydrogen runs out → red giant (hydrogen shell fusion, then helium → carbon and oxygen) → planetary nebula → white dwarf, held up by electron degeneracy pressure.
  • Above about 8 solar masses: red supergiant, fusing heavier elements in layers up to iron → iron releases no energy, the core collapses → supernova (elements heavier than iron made and scattered) → neutron star or black hole.
  • The Sun's path on the HR diagram: main sequence → up and right to red giants → across and down to white dwarfs.

New for 2028 The role of the limits (they apply to the mass of the core left behind, not the original star):

Remnant core massHeld up byEnd point
below 1.4 $M_\odot$ (Chandrasekhar limit)electron degeneracy pressurewhite dwarf
1.4 to about 2–3 $M_\odot$ (Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit)neutron degeneracy pressureneutron star
above about 2–3 $M_\odot$nothingblack hole

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Reading the HR temperature axis the wrong way: it increases to the left.
  • Calling a light year a time.
  • Using the full angular shift as the parallax angle: $p$ is half of it.
  • Forgetting to square $R$ or raise $T$ to the fourth power; using °C instead of K.
  • Saying stars are held up by a fusion "explosion": they are in equilibrium.
  • Thinking massive stars live longer because they have more fuel.
  • Saying white dwarfs still fuse: they are just cooling.
  • Applying the Chandrasekhar limit to the star's main-sequence mass instead of its remnant core.

Measurement: Bessel's parallax was about a third of an arcsecond. Ask students to work out how big that angle is, for example the distance at which a 2 cm coin would look that small (about 13 km).
For centuries, no measurable parallax was used as evidence that the Earth doesn't move. What was wrong with that argument?
Collaboration: Cannon's classification needed years of careful human judgement. Which parts of that work could a computer do today, and which still need people?
The Harvard "computers" were mostly women, poorly paid and often under-recognised. How has the recognition of this work changed?
Patterns: Give students a table of stars' luminosities and temperatures and let them plot it before naming the regions. What groups do they find?
Does finding a pattern explain anything, or only show what needs explaining?
Technology: Gaia measured over a billion parallaxes. How does a dataset that size change the questions astronomers can ask?
Why can a space telescope measure angles that ground-based telescopes can't?

oracy.html:
Talk tokens (fours, 10 minutes), with a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram on the desk: each student spends a token to add each point; nobody speaks again until everyone has spent one. Claim: "A star with a higher surface temperature than the Sun must also be more luminous."

  • On the diagram, …
  • That fits with …, because …
  • I'd challenge that, because …

Listen for: $L = \sigma AT^4$, so luminosity depends on surface area as well as temperature; white dwarfs are hotter than the Sun but far less luminous, because they are so small.

Can we understand what we can't imagine?: Build a scale model: if the Sun were a grain of sand, where would the nearest star be? Does the model help, or just replace one unimaginable number with another?
Is understanding a number the same as being able to calculate with it?
How can we study a process we can't watc: Compare the HR diagram with working out how trees grow by photographing a forest once. What assumptions does the method need?
Which other subjects rebuild long processes from snapshots (geology, evolution, history)?
Who decides what is \"real\"?: Payne-Gaposchkin was persuaded to call her result "almost certainly not real". What should a young scientist do when the data contradict senior experts?
Is consensus a good guide to truth? When has it been right, and when wrong?
Is the light we see the star we think it: Ask students how long ago the light left the Sun, the nearest star and a galaxy. Are we seeing these objects or their history?
If every observation shows the past, can we know anything about the universe as it is now?
